newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat to meet U.S. envoy Ross on Hebron accord.
newsitem.headline: Arafat to meet U.S. envoy Ross on Hebron accord.

text.p: U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross was to meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in Gaza late on Monday in an effort to clinch an accord on the handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule.
"Ross will meet with Arafat at midnight (2200 GMT)," said a Palestinian official who did not want to be identified. He said Arafat would meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday.

Ross was to travel to Gaza from Jerusalem, where he earlier on Monday joined Israeli and Palestinian negotiators trying to finalise an accord on a handover of most of Hebron to Palestinian rule. Before entering the negotiations Ross conferred with Netanyahu.
"There is work going on. There is still a lot of work to be done," the U.S. envoy told reporters in Jerusalem.
Asked if a Hebron agreement was close Ross said: "I think there are still issues to be resolved. I think you should focus on the fact that there is more work to be done."
Ross, who has shuttled between Israel, PLO-ruled Gaza and Egypt, arrived in the region on Saturday saying he hoped to re-energise the talks.
Palestinian chief negotiator Mahmoud Abbas, also known as Abu Mazen, said the talks had reached a critical stage.
"I am going to Gaza to consult with President (Yasser) Arafat. We are at a critical stage now," he said, adding that progress had been made.
Asked if he had a copy of a Hebron agreement with him, Abbas said: "I am taking with me the general guidelines to inform President Arafat about what has been reached until now."
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai told reporters on Monday that Israel was "more optimistic" now about a deal.

In Hebron, an Israeli truck took camp beds and equipment from the military governor's office but officials declined to say whether final preparations for a long-delayed troop redeployment were under way.
Only six military vehicles were left at the building, the nerve centre of Israel's military occupation of Hebron since 1967, reporters said.

Palestinian officials had said there was agreement on some major disputed points, but other issues were left to be resolved in a meeting yet to be arranged between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

Israel and the PLO have accused each other of foot-dragging in more than three months of talks on Hebron, 80 percent of which was due to have been handed over to Arafat's Palestinian Authority months ago.

Netanyahu, who came to power in June vowing to take a tough line on Israeli security, has demanded protection for 400 Jewish militants in the heart of the city of 100,000 Arabs, a longtime flashpoint of violence between Arabs and Jews.

PLO officials said the Israelis had dropped their insistence on having the right of hot pursuit of Palestinian suspects into PLO-held areas, accepting instead existing language in the Hebron handover agreement signed in 1995.
One PLO official said agreement had also been reached to reopen Martyrs Street in the heart of the town within four months. It has been closed to Palestinians.
It was also agreed to reopen the long-closed vegetable market so long as it was a retail rather than a wholesale market, he said.
